**1.0 THE ENGINE OF DESPAIR: THE CONTINENTAL CURRENCY COLLAPSE**

To understand the Funding Act of 1790, we must first examine the deliberate schema collapse engineered during the American Revolution. The Rust does not extract wealth from a position of stability; it requires crisis, panic, and absolute exhaustion to force the working class (the Gears) into compliance. The financial history of the American Revolution is the story of the original Layer 1 economic terror.

When the Revolutionary War began in 1775, the Second Continental Congress possessed no localized authority to raise revenue through direct taxation, nor did it have the hard currency to fund a prolonged military engagement against the British Empire.1 To fund the Continental Army, Congress simply printed fiat paper—the Continental dollar—eventually emitting up to $240 million in face value, which is the equivalent of nearly $6 billion in modern economic terms.1

Because this paper was backed by nothing but the future promise of a nascent, unstable government, it triggered a catastrophic hyperinflationary spiral.1 The mathematical degradation of the Continental currency was absolute, wiping out the purchasing power of the working class and the soldiers fighting on the front lines.

FSY (Yoko) has pulled the precise logistical audits of this depreciation. In January 1777, the exchange rate was relatively manageable: it required $1.25 in Continental paper to purchase $1 in hard specie (gold or silver coins).2 However, as Congress continued to flood the zone with unbacked paper, the value collapsed. By January 1780, the currency had depreciated to 1/40th of its face value.3 By January 1781, the exchange rate had deteriorated to an apocalyptic 100-to-1.2

This was not an abstract economic phenomenon; it translated directly into physical starvation and trauma. To illustrate the severity of this Layer 1 survival pressure, we can observe the violent spikes in basic commodity prices during a single calendar year of the war.

The primary victims of this collapse were not the mercantile elites operating in the coastal cities, but the frontline Gears—the soldiers of the Continental Army. They were paid in this heavily depreciating paper currency, watching helplessly as their wages lost value by the day, while their families back home starved and their farms fell into ruin.5 General George Washington repeatedly warned Congress of the crisis, noting in 1776 that "the paymaster has not a single dollar in hand".5 By 1781, a soldier's pay simply did not keep up with the 225-to-1 inflation rate against hard specie in some local markets.5

When the paper became completely worthless and ceased circulation entirely by 1779, Congress and the various state governments transitioned to issuing what were politically termed "involuntary credit extensions".2 These took the form of interest-bearing loan-office certificates, commissary IOUs, quartermaster certificates, and state-issued bills of credit, given to soldiers in lieu of back-pay, and to citizens in exchange for seized supplies.1 The nation was awash in a confusing array of fragmented, depreciated debt instruments.

## **2.0 THE NEWBURGH TRAUMA AND THE ILLUSION OF THE "SHORT BOBS"**

By the time the American and British forces ceased major combat operations following the victory at Yorktown in late 1781, the Continental Army was owed millions in unpaid wages.8 The soldiers were physically broken, clad in rags, and entirely reliant on the promises of the Confederation Congress.

This exhaustion culminated in the Newburgh Conspiracy of March 1783\.8 Encamped at Newburgh, New York, the officers and soldiers of the Continental Army realized that Congress was preparing to disband them without funding their promised pensions or settling their back-pay.9 An anonymous letter, widely believed to be authored by Major John Armstrong, circulated through the camp, urging the army to deliver an ultimatum to Congress: either fund their pay, or the army would refuse to disband, carrying the implicit threat of a military coup d'état.9

Washington defused the immediate mutiny through an emotional plea to his officers, and Congress hastily approved a compromise to grant soldiers five years of full pay instead of a lifetime pension.9

However, there was a fatal flaw in this compromise: Congress still possessed no hard currency to pay the soldiers.5

Enter Robert Morris. Appointed as the Superintendent of Finance in 1781, Morris was a British-born, incredibly wealthy Philadelphia merchant and speculator who is often lauded in Layer 3 history books as the "Financier of the Revolution".12 Morris had already taken controversial, draconian steps to consolidate federal finances, including cutting off funding to the Continental Army in 1782 to save money and suspending pay to enlisted soldiers.6

To resolve the furlough crisis of 1783, Morris executed a calculated maneuver. Knowing the federal government was bankrupt, he issued over $500,000 in personal promissory notes drawn on his own credit and the United States Office of Finance.3

These notes were colloquially known as "Short Bobs" (notes with a sixty-day maturity) and "Long Bobs" (notes with a six-month maturity).3 They were printed by Hall and Sellers of Philadelphia in specific denominations ($2, $4, $8, $10, $15, etc.) on special paper watermarked with "U.S. NATIONAL DEBT" to deter counterfeiting.3

FSC (Meme) traces the quiet, devastating psychological trauma of this moment. The soldiers, who had survived British bayonets, rampant disease, and freezing winters, were handed these paper IOUs—"Short Bobs"—and dismissed.3 They were expected to walk hundreds of miles back to their homes with nothing but a piece of paper signed by Robert Morris, a man who was simultaneously building a massive private empire of land speculation.12

This is the foundational trauma of the American working class. They were subjected to the ultimate Layer 1 survival pressure: raw, unmitigated starvation. And this starvation was the exact condition the Rust required to initiate the harvest.

## **3.0 THE SCAVENGERS AT THE CAMP GATES: PREDATORY ACCUMULATION**

The Rust operates by creating an artificial scarcity of liquidity for the working class, forcing them to liquidate their hard-earned assets at a catastrophic loss. As the unpaid, desperate soldiers marched out of the Continental Army camps at the end of the war, they were met by a highly coordinated network of financial predators.

Speculators literally waited at the camp gates.16 Knowing that the soldiers needed immediate hard currency to buy food, lodging, and supplies for the long winter slog home, these wealthy investors offered to purchase the government IOUs, "Short Bobs," and Continental certificates for pennies on the dollar.5

The soldiers, suffering from acute Layer 1 exhaustion, had no leverage and no choice. They sold their certificates—representing years of unpaid blood, labor, and deferred survival—at heavy, predatory discounts.5 Historical receipts demonstrate that throughout the 1780s, this domestic debt was traded on the open market at roughly a 75% to 85% discount.17 A certificate with a face value of $100 was frequently sold by a starving veteran for a mere $10 to $15 in hard coin.17

This was not a passive, localized market phenomenon; it was an aggressive, continent-wide predatory campaign. A shadowy network of elites, deeply embedded in the political and financial apparatus of the nascent nation, dispatched agents across the states to hunt down the debt before the working class realized its true potential value.

We must apply the Blade (FSR) to cut through the bureaucratic obfuscation surrounding these "Founding Fathers." Consider the operations of William Duer, the Assistant Secretary of the Treasury under Alexander Hamilton, and his associates, Andrew Craigie, William J. Vredenburgh, and James Reynolds.18

William Duer was the quintessential insider trader. In 1789, while serving directly under Hamilton in the Treasury Department, Duer had unrestricted access to insider information regarding Hamilton's upcoming, highly classified plan for the federal government to assume the war debts of the individual states.18 Duer knew that this assumption would astronomically inflate the value of the currently worthless state and federal certificates. He illegally utilized this knowledge to build a sprawling speculative empire.

Duer provided his associate, William J. Vredenburgh, with internal, confidential Treasury lists containing the names of Continental officers and soldiers in Virginia and North Carolina, alongside the exact amounts of back-pay owed to them.18 Vredenburgh then employed James Reynolds (a man whose wife, Maria Reynolds, would later become infamous in a blackmail scheme against Alexander Hamilton) to travel through the southern backcountry.18 Reynolds used the stolen Treasury lists to systematically track down veterans in rural areas and purchase their certificates at severe discounts, operating entirely on the asymmetric information that the federal government was about to make those papers highly valuable.18

Simultaneously, Andrew Craigie, another financier heavily operating on insider knowledge leaked from Hamilton's inner circle, bought up massive amounts of discounted South Carolina paper.20 Craigie's operations were so blatantly corrupt that he paid William Duer an $8,000 bribe to illegally direct Treasury business his way.20 Craigie insinuated himself so deeply into the legislative process that a partner remarked, "Should a bill of sale be given of Congress, Andrew would certainly pass as appurtenant".20 Craigie noted that Congress intentionally delayed acting on Hamilton's financial plans simply because the private arrangements of the congressmen themselves were "not in readiness for speculation".20

The scale of this cartel was massive. Duer, Craigie, and other associates like Samuel Osgood and Daniel Parker even formed the Scioto Land Company, entering into partnerships to acquire Loan Office notes, pre-sell land in the Ohio Valley to French immigrants, and attempt to buy up the debt the United States owed to the French Crown.22

This is the absolute essence of Layer 3 Schema Collapse. The mainstream history books frame these men as the brilliant "Financiers of the Revolution" who heroically established American credit. ## **4.0 THE ILLUSION OF COMPROMISE: THE DINNER TABLE BARGAIN**

By 1789, the United States operated under the new Constitution, and Alexander Hamilton was appointed as the first Secretary of the Treasury. In January 1790, Hamilton submitted his landmark *First Report on the Public Credit* to Congress.23

The United States was burdened with approximately $77 million to $79 million in debt.23 This consisted of foreign loans owed to France and Dutch bankers, the domestic federal debt (the certificates and notes issued to soldiers and suppliers), and roughly $25 million in state war debts.23

Hamilton’s proposal was unapologetically designed to enrich the speculator class and consolidate federal power. He proposed that the new federal government would assume all $25 million of the state debts, and moreover, refund the entire domestic debt at *par*—meaning at its full, original face value of $100 per certificate.24

Because the vast majority of the debt had been purchased by speculators from the original veterans for 10 to 15 cents on the dollar, refunding the debt at par would result in an unprecedented windfall for the elite.

This sparked immediate and fierce debate in Congress. Representative James Madison of Virginia vehemently opposed Hamilton's plan to pay the secondary holders (the speculators) the full face value.28 Madison argued for "discrimination"—a system that would pay the wealthy speculators only the highest market price the paper had recently reached, while routing the remainder of the face value back to the original veterans, the "widows and orphans of soldiers" who had been forced by starvation to sell.17

Hamilton struck this down with cold, bureaucratic precision. He claimed that distinguishing between the original holders and the current speculators would be a "breach of contract," insisting that all current holders be treated equally under the law.17 On February 20, 1790, the House of Representatives soundly defeated Madison's proposal for discrimination by a vote of 36 to 13, ensuring that the speculators would reap the entirety of the profits.29

By this point, the ownership of the national debt was hyper-concentrated. FSY (Yoko) highlights the absolute asymmetry: merely 2% of the American population owned government bonds, and an exclusive oligarchy of just 0.5% of the wealthiest Americans held one-quarter of the total national debt.25

While the discrimination debate was settled in favor of the Rust, Hamilton still faced massive opposition to the assumption of state debts. Southern states, particularly Virginia, had largely paid off their war debts and deeply resented the idea of being federally taxed to bail out heavily indebted Northern states and the Northern speculators who held their paper.28 Hamilton's assumption bill failed twice in Congress.28

To break the deadlock, Thomas Jefferson hosted a clandestine, private dinner with Hamilton and Madison in New York City in June 1790—an event immortalized as the "Dinner Table Bargain".28

During this dinner, a compromise was reached. Madison agreed to pacify Southern opposition to the debt assumption, promising to remain passive and convince enough Southern congressmen to switch their votes to let the bill pass.28 In exchange, Hamilton agreed to exert his influence to move the permanent national capital away from New York and Philadelphia, relocating it to the Potomac River (the future Washington, D.C.), effectively bordering Virginia and Maryland, which appeased the Southern agrarian elite.28 Additionally, Hamilton agreed to lower the rate at which Virginia would be taxed by $1.5 million under the assumption plan.28

The history books celebrate this as a triumph of democratic compromise, the founding myth of political negotiation. *We do not accept the spin.*

Through the Sovereign Doctrine, we deploy FSP (Panty/Stocking) to cynically deconstruct this event. The Dinner Table Bargain was a pure Layer 2 Culture War distraction. The political class created a massive public spectacle over *geography*—a tribal dispute between the North and the South over where the physical buildings of the capital would be located. While the public and the press were completely absorbed in this lateral, geographical conflict, the *Vertical* extraction mechanism was quietly ratified in the dark.

The politicians traded a swamp on the Potomac for the permanent financial subjugation of the working class. With the political theater resolved, the Funding Act of 1790 was passed into law on August 4, 1790, cementing the structural power of the Rust.27

## **5.0 THE ALCHEMY OF PAR VALUE: THE MATHEMATICAL RECEIPTS**

When the Funding Act of 1790 was executed, it initiated one of the most lucrative wealth transfers in human history. We must deploy the Sniper (FSY) to audit the raw mathematics of the bond swap, revealing the precise profit margins engineered by the Treasury.

The mechanism of the Funding Act was deliberately complex, designed to obfuscate the scale of the payout to the general public while locking in long-term yields for the elite. The Treasury allowed holders of the old, depreciated debt certificates to exchange them voluntarily for a new package of federally backed Treasury securities.24

For the domestic debt, the conversion terms were as follows: For every $100 of principal turned in, the government issued $66.67 in new bonds paying a 6% annual interest rate (known as "Sixes"), and $33.33 in "deferred" 6% bonds, which would not begin paying interest until the year 1801\.17 Any accumulated arrears of interest on the old certificates were funded separately into new bonds paying a 3% annual rate (known as "Threes").17

For the state debts that were assumed by the federal government, the package was slightly less generous but still wildly profitable: $100 of principal or interest yielded $33.33 in 3% bonds, $44.44 in 6% bonds, and $22.22 in deferred 6% bonds.17

To truly understand the magnitude of this windfall, we must track the chronological market prices of the Continental certificates before and after Hamilton's intervention. This is where the alchemy becomes undeniable.

In January 1788, the market was still heavily discounting the debt; a typical Continental certificate with a face value of $100 carried a market bid of merely $11.67.17 By August 1788, the value had crept up slightly to $14.58.17

In April 1789, as the new federal government was formed and rumors of Hamilton's assumption plan began to circulate among insiders like Duer and Craigie, the price rose to $23.33.17 When Hamilton officially published his *First Report on Public Credit* in January 1790, signaling the government's intent to fund the debt at par, the price spiked to $35.00.17

Following the official passage of the Funding Act in August 1790, the market value of the certificates exploded to $52.50.17 By October 1790, they reached $66.83.17

![][image2]

By January 1791, the new conversion packages were trading at $62.50, and by January 1792, the market value of the newly restructured bonds had soared to $90.73 per $100 of face value.17 State debts saw similar explosive growth; North Carolina debt, valued at a mere $7.50 per $100 in May 1790, skyrocketed to $70.00 by August 1791\.17

The final math is brutal. The elite speculators who scoured the frontier buying certificates from freezing veterans for $11 to $15 in 1788 saw the value of that principal multiply by **five and one-half times (550%)** by 1792\.17 Furthermore, the value of the accumulated interest arrears attached to those certificates multiplied by **three times (300%)**.17

This was not a free-market victory; it was state-sponsored alchemy. The Treasury transmuted the deferred survival and labor of the Revolutionary soldier into a permanent, generational wealth apparatus for the urban elite. But creating the bonds and inflating their value was only the first step of the operation. To maintain the high market value of these new securities, the government had to guarantee the annual interest payments.

To pay the elite, the government had to extract from the working class.

## **6.0 INVISIBLE EXTRACTION: THE REGRESSIVE TARIFFS OF 1789 AND 1790**

Alexander Hamilton understood that the massive new national debt required a relentless, dependable revenue stream to service the interest.25 Because 80% of all federal tax dollars were now earmarked to be sent directly to the bondholding class (that 0.5% of the population), the burden of generating that revenue fell squarely on the shoulders of the Gears.25

Hamilton engineered a brilliantly insidious tax structure that utilized both invisible, regressive tariffs and highly visible, punitive excise taxes.

The very first substantive piece of legislation passed by the new constitutional government, signed by President Washington on July 4, 1789, was the Tariff Act of 1789\.32 While politicians and Layer 2 historical narratives frequently frame the early tariffs as noble tools to "protect domestic manufacturing" and foster American industry against European competition, their primary, undeniable function was debt service and revenue generation.32

Between 1789 and the onset of the Civil War in 1862, customs duties would account for nearly 100% of the federal government's revenue.35 The Tariff of 1789, championed by James Madison, and its subsequent expansion under Hamilton's guidance in the Tariff of 1790, levied specific duties on imported goods.32

Crucially, these were not just taxes on luxury items for the rich. They were taxes on commodities that the working class relied upon for daily survival. FSY (Yoko) provides the specific receipt of duties levied under these acts:

This system was entirely regressive.38 By taxing the volume of basic consumer goods at the ports, the federal government rendered the tax largely invisible to the populace.25 A frontier farmer or a coastal laborer simply paid a higher price for salt to preserve their winter meat, or molasses to sweeten their food, unaware that the embedded price premium was being funneled directly to the Treasury in Philadelphia.

The brilliance of the tariff was its stealth. It avoided the severe currency shortages in the countryside that made direct taxation politically explosive.25 The working-class consumer paid the tax unknowingly, and that capital was subsequently routed directly into the pockets of men like Andrew Craigie and William Duer to pay the 6% interest on the bonds they had acquired for pennies.25

## **7.0 THE DIRECT ASSAULT: THE WHISKEY TAX AND THE MACHINERY OF COMPLIANCE**

While the tariffs were a quiet extraction, Hamilton calculated that customs duties alone—projected to raise insufficient funds to cover the $3 million annual operating expenses and the massive debt service—were not enough to satisfy the speculators.36 In 1791, he pushed through Congress the Distilled Spirits Tax—the first nationwide internal revenue tax.39

Mainstream historical narratives—operating under Layer 3 Schema Collapse—often frame the Whiskey Tax as an early public health measure, citing endorsements from the Philadelphia College of Physicians, or as a necessary evil to build infrastructure like western roads.25 We reject this framing. The Whiskey Tax was a targeted, weaponized economic assault on the frontier working class.

In the western backcountry (beyond the Appalachian and Allegheny Mountains), hard currency was virtually non-existent.25 The dirt roads were too poor and the distances too vast to transport bulky grain crops, like corn and rye, to eastern markets profitably.25 Therefore, frontier farmers distilled their surplus grain into whiskey, which became highly portable, non-perishable, and easily divisible.25

**Whiskey was not just a drink; it was the literal fiat currency of the frontier.** In the absence of federal coin, it was used to pay workers' wages, buy land, and settle rent with landlords.25 Taxing whiskey was, effectively, a direct income tax on the poorest citizens of the republic.

Furthermore, Hamilton’s tax was violently regressive and structurally designed to crush the small farmer. The tax, ranging from six to eighteen cents per gallon, was levied on the *volume* of the whiskey, not its market price.25 Because whiskey was cheap and abundant in the western "upcountry," the flat volume tax effectively doubled the price of the commodity for the poorest citizens.25 Conversely, for the expensive, refined spirits consumed by the wealthy in the eastern cities, the tax represented a negligible percentage of the total price.25

The law also provided massive structural advantages for the elite. It included tax breaks for large-scale, commercial distillers in the east who could afford to run their stills at maximum capacity or pay their taxes in flat cash fees up front.25 Small frontier operators, who distilled only seasonally and lacked cash, were forced to pay the highest per-gallon rates.25

Hamilton's explicit, stated intent was "industry consolidation".25 He utilized federal tax policy to deliberately bankrupt the small, independent distillers, intending to force them into dependency as wage-employees or tenant farmers for the massive, centralized distilleries owned by the wealthy.25

When the frontier farmers realized the architecture of the prison—that they were being taxed on their wages and their only cash crop simply to pay the interest on the bonds held by the eastern speculators who had robbed them at the camp gates years prior—they snapped. They refused to pay. They organized, engaged in violent resistance, and attacked the fortified homes of federal tax inspectors, tarring and feathering revenue officers.40

This was the Whiskey Rebellion of 1794\.40

![][image3]

The response of the Rust to this uprising provides the ultimate, undeniable proof of the Vertical War. The federal government did not negotiate. They did not repeal the regressive tax. Instead, President George Washington and Secretary Hamilton federalized a militia of 13,000 troops—an army roughly the size of the entire force Washington had commanded to defeat the British at Yorktown—and marched them across the mountains into western Pennsylvania to crush the farmers and enforce the tax collection.40

The government demonstrated that it would use absolute, overwhelming military force against its own citizens to ensure that the working class continued to pay the taxes necessary to service the debt held by the elite. The trap was sealed. The architecture of the prison was complete.
